text: Once aboard the Annabelle, that's the only way you'll get off her. Straight downwards.
Room enough for rebels, get stoned below!
What have you got down here, stinking fish?
That's exactly what it is, stinking fish!
Yes you are, you scabby swamp!
I don't mind letting you, I'll be down here with my cutlass.
You'll learn who's master you are.
It'll be no better from being cooped up in this hell hole.
Hey Mike, got any idea where they're sending us?
One more blow and we can strike for Scotland!
One more piece of vermin to be starved out!
Put a foot of him in and tramp his English bones into the deck!
The first blow will be mine!
We must strike a friend of the Prince!
You haven't been away so long, you don't recognise me!
And Jamie, son of Donald MacCrimmon.
A piper, like his father and his father's father.
We're no pipes though, just my chanter.
But this Englishman, he is a friend to our Prince.
He helped bring me here, weak but alive.
Oh, well now, I crave your pardon.
A friend of the McLarens is a friend of mine.
Well, thanks, I'm glad to hear it.
But how came he here with you?
Yeah, that's what we're thinking back home.
I'm a man of the sea myself.
The master of this very vessel.
If you're a skipper here, what's that Trask geezer doing on the bridge?
I was running arms from France past a blockade.
The navy boarded the Annabelle and now he's sailing the ship for King George.
Oh, no, skipper, just a bit about working for King George.
Well, we're not exactly being treated like prisoners of war now, are we?
Hasn't it occurred to you that this Trask could be using this vessel without the knowledge of his king and sovereign in order to work some big fiddle on his own account?
Look, mate, he is going to sell us like the stinking fish he thinks we are.
That's what we're going to be, slave labour.
Bestie, you gave me such a fright.
I'm not used to fetching and carrying.
You know, we used to have our own servants.
Aye, the clothes for you and the trays and oranges.
What do we have to spend the money on oranges for?
Last time we went back to the past, I had to wear boys' clothes all the time.
Now then, how do I look?
The next thing is the oranges.
You're not going to have us selling oranges, are you?
Well, I haven't got it wrong, have I?
You do have orange sellers, don't you?
I mean, Nell Gwynn and all that.
Well, of course there are orange sellers in Scotland.
But they're mostly coarse common girls.
The sort that hang around soldiers.
Right, then we're going to be orange sellers.
Well, look, how else can we find out where they've taken the doctor and your father?
Always assuming he's got out of that terrible pit.
In here and see the officer.
I am fine with both of you.
They still look like the rebels we were searching for yesterday, sir.
Well, that's all, Sergeant. Be about your business.
All right, you scum, out of it!
The king doesn't pay you while you're around here any more!
Off with your mouth, all of you!
The last one up gets 500 lashes!
Oh, Algy, we thought you'd be flattered.
We turned to you for help immediately, didn't we, Kerstin?
Just the sort of man two defenceless girls would turn to.
I'll have you thrown in prison.
What more do you want from me?
Step me of taking all my money?
I haven't even the price of a glass of wine left on me.
I don't suppose the doctor and the others have a glass of water to drink,
never mind wine. Now, where are they?
What should I know? In prison, I expect, where they belong.
They're not to have checked. Now, where are they?
I don't know! I just round them up.
I'll have to ask Solicitor Grey. He's in charge of prisoners, not me.
He's got a room somewhere near here.
I should have had a wink of sleep yet.
Two wenches there to see the Solicitor.
Is Cedric Perkins, Solicitor's clerk, ladies, at your service?
What can I do for you?
Giving some rebel prisoners the choice between life and death.
Solicitor wills that a choir is pointed at a choir.
The Solicitor hath news for him.
A mark of clemency from His Most Gracious Majesty, King George.
It is pleased His Majesty to declare
that whereas there are a great many of his rebellious subjects in jail,
a speedy example must be made of them.
Therefore it is ordained that there will be those required as witnesses.
Those not wanting to turn King's evidence will be hanged.
Plantation workers are required to work in His Majesty's colonies in the West Indies.
Sign your names to these, and you will receive free transportation to your new homes.
Well, which of you lucky lads will be the first to sign?
I know fine what you offer, Mr. Solicitor.
I have seen these plantations in the Indies.
Not one of you men that signs will live out your seven years.
Better a quick and honorable death at the end of the rope
than a long, slow one after months of battle.
William McCoy, former master of this vessel.
I should have dumped for him long ago.
Listen to me, all of you.
You've heard what Mackay here offers you.
Lingering on the end of a halter?
Followed, may I remind you, by quartering and the like, courtesies extended to rebels.
I offer you life and a chance to work for your eventual liberty.
Unless, of course, Mr. McCoy, you would care to turn King's evidence.
For the rest of you, for those who wish to sign, over here.
For those who wish to hang, over there.
Get those witnesses on the contract.
Let him go, let him go.
I'm not Scots, but can I sign?
When I return with new contracts, we'll bind him and drop him from the highest yarder.
The next man who tries to oppose me will not be so fortunate.
Mr. Grey doesn't seem to be coming.
I think we'd better be off.
Oh, surely, ladies, you won't deprive an old fellow of your charming company?
Very well, I shall rouse the watch.
They may be interested in two such genteel orange wenches.
Now, to pass the time, what say you to a nice round of whist?
There's nothing nicer than a nice game of whist.
Perhaps you'd like to cut for trumps?
Would you like to deal with the body orange wench?
What the devil are you at, man?
Just playing a round of cards, Mr. Grey.
Then you can just come up to my room.
You wouldn't want another headache now, would you?
I tell you what we're going to do.
We ladies are going to leave first.
But you are going to sit here quietly, comfortably for another ten minutes.
I take care of him before you leave because I am going to watch you all the time.
That is how I understand, sir.
Now, girls, let's leave this rough place.

Doctor! Doctor! Have you got a plan for us?
Oh, go on. I know you better than that. You must have a plan.
Well, it's just a wee idea, really.
I've only just thought about it. It won't work. But it'd be a try. Anyone got any money?
Yes. 17 guineas that we picked from the English lieutenant.
That's a fortune in these days. Now, we want weapons, lots of them, and a rowing boat.
I can get a rowing boat.
Good. And we can buy the weapons.
From the English soldiers. Well, they're bound to have heaps of weapons as souvenirs.
Yes, but will they sell them to us?
You don't know the English soldier. He'd sell his grandmother for top and safety.
We smuggle them aboard the Annabelle.
Oh, I don't know. We'll think of something. I must get some sleep.
Oh, take it ready for that.
Ah, you. Go fetch Mr. Trask.
I've had Perkins, here. Copy out three contracts, just to make sure.
But if anyone tries that trick again of tearing them up I'll shoot him down immediately.
We need two of the contracts to be signed.
Every man, every man, jack for no sign, is not willing to come with blood.
This is all the one to me.
You're not dealing with slaves, ma'am.
These Highlanders are men of high courage and resolution.
They'll all stand together and refuse to sign a thing.
You'll undo everything I've worked for.
They can be whipped to death for all I care.
Until then, use a light fist, or you'll answer to me.
It'll serve as a useful encouragement to the rest.
Perkins, go below, make the preparations.
And Perkins, bring the deserter on deck today.
We haven't done very well, have we?
I do hope the doctor's had better.
Must have robbed the Duke's arsenal.
She won't let you touch it.
Then why has it the Stuart seal?
My father bade me not tell where he got it.
The prince gave it to my father off his own hand in the heat of battle.
My father saved the prince's life.
Then it is right and proper that it should now save his life.
